name: Neem twig / miswak
lead: Chewing sticks are twigs whose frayed ends are used as natural toothbrushes. The best known is miswak, from the Salvadora persica tree, traditionally used in the Middle East; neem (Azadirachta indica) twigs are commonly used the same way in southern India and the Middle East [1][2].

Believers cite tradition, antibacterial compounds and plaque control. A WHO recommendation in 1986 was followed by a 2000 consensus report saying more research was needed [1]. Some observational studies link use with better gum status, but they are small [1].

paras: The outer bark is peeled to expose fibers that act as bristles, and the end can be trimmed to renew the brushing surface [1]. Hadith are reported to recommend its use, and fibrous chewing sticks have been used since antiquity [1].

Salvadorine and benzylisothiocyanate are believed to be responsible for miswak antibacterial activity, and it contains insoluble fluoride, calcium and salicylic acid [1]. Neem products have a long history in Indian traditional medicine, but the neem article states insufficient clinical evidence for medicinal benefits [2].

A study of 203 people in Sudan found better periodontal status in miswak users than toothbrush users, and a study of 480 Saudi adults linked frequent use to lower need for periodontal treatment [1]. Lab work found miswak extract less antimicrobial than chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium mouthrinses [1]. No studies of tooth whitening were found; for peroxide whitening see [3].
Neem oil is described as toxic to small children, and neem may be associated with miscarriage, infertility and low blood sugar [2]; these concern ingestion of products rather than twig chewing.

timeline.event: An international consensus report says more research is needed on its effects [1]

card.summary: Traditional chewing sticks with a long history; small observational studies on gum health, no whitening trials.
card.note: Evidence is observational; no whitening trials.

quick.overview:
Miswak and neem twigs are chewing sticks used as natural toothbrushes, especially in the Middle East and South Asia.

Small observational studies link miswak use to better gum health; no trials of whitening were found.
quick.mechanism: The frayed fibers clean mechanically, and plant compounds are believed to have antibacterial activity.
quick.risks: Twig chewing has no specific harms in the sources reviewed; neem oil is toxic to small children.
